name: Diego Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a business degree in Birmingham. I get up early, because I help my uncle load the van on Saturday mornings, and during the week it's lectures, the library, and a quick dinner at the flat. On Sundays I go to church with my parents, then eat with the whole family, which can be fifteen people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the family business, and why you chose this degree.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents run a food wholesale firm with four lorries and about thirty staff. My grandfather started it from a market stall. I'm doing business so I can take it over one day and run it better, and I want to learn the books properly. The family pays all my costs, I've no debt, and I've never used one of those AI tools, because I like to see how a thing works first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought. A new gadget, and a lot of fuss. I'd tell the family, over Sunday lunch, that nothing changes and we keep doing what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel settled. We run on trust, handshakes and knowing which café needs what on which day. Software helps a bit with orders, but a lorry still has to get there. My own worry would be the same as it is now: the margins on food are thin, and a bad year can hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd study, work Saturdays with my uncle, and learn the firm's books during the holidays. I'd also talk to my dad about the thin margins and whether we're charging enough, because that's the real risk, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the ordinary worry of a family firm, but nothing new. I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the real risk to the firm, in your own words?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the real risk to the firm, in your own words? Fuel prices, a big customer going under, and a good driver leaving. We had a driver, Mr. Hossain, who retired last year, and it took six months to replace him, so I think about that more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the AI hype turned out to be real after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the AI hype did turn out to be real? I'd look at it with my dad before we bought anything. We'd test it on one small job, like ordering, and see if it saves us money, not just time. We'd test any new tool on one small job, like ordering, and see whether it saves us money and not just time.

say: I'd tell the family over Sunday lunch that it's **a gadget**, nothing more, and a fuss.
think: The firm runs on **trust and handshakes**, and a lorry still has to arrive.
My real worry is **thin margins**, not AI.
do: Study, work Saturdays with my uncle and learn the firm's **books** in holidays.
Talk to my dad about **margins** and pricing.
feel: **Calm**: only the ordinary worries of a family firm.
S0.quote: We'd test any new tool on one small job, like ordering, and see whether it saves us money and not just time.
fieldNote: Diego's calm comes from his **family firm's** trust-based, physical work.
He names risks that are not AI: fuel, big customers and losing a good driver.

steps.text: Work Saturdays with my uncle loading the van
Learn the firm's books during the holidays
Test any new tool on one small job before buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and change has always come, and good businesses adapt. I'd tell people not to complain but to learn. I'd also say big firms shouldn't use it to cut people just to look clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel uneasy about the office side of the firm. Orders, invoices and customer calls are the sort of thing the card says goes first. My aunt does the accounts and my cousin does orders, and I'd wonder what happens to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad to try one tool for orders, with someone showing us how. I'd learn the basics myself, since I'd need to if I'm going to run the place. I'd also keep the drivers and warehouse team as they are, because the card says robots reach hands-on work later. I'd save more from my Saturday pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't enjoy new tools, but I'd rather learn than get left behind. Feeling for my aunt and cousin is the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if office jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you blame if office jobs go? Mostly the big tech companies selling it as magic, and the big chains who'll use it to squeeze small suppliers. Not the workers, never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect your aunt's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you protect your aunt's job? By moving her to something the software can't do, like handling our biggest customers directly. She's good with people, and the customers like her. The tools will do orders and invoices, but my aunt knows every customer by name, and the software never will.

say: I'd say **change has always come**, and good firms adapt.
I'd warn that big firms shouldn't use it just to **cut people**.
think: The firm's **office side** is exposed: orders, invoices and customer calls.
My **aunt and cousin** work there, and I'd wonder about them.
do: Try one **ordering tool** with someone showing us how, and learn the basics.
Keep the drivers and warehouse team and **save more** of my Saturday pay.
feel: **Uneasy**: he dislikes new tools but would rather learn than be left behind.
S1.quote: The tools will do orders and invoices, but my aunt knows every customer by name, and the software never will.
fieldNote: Diego's concern is **personal and specific**: relatives in the office jobs the card names.
He blames big tech and large chains, and explicitly not workers.

steps.text: Try one ordering tool in the firm with someone showing us how
Learn the basics of the tool myself
Move my aunt to handling our biggest customers directly
Save more of my Saturday pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster waiting to happen if the government and big firms treat it like a game. I'd say small firms and ordinary workers need protection first. At church and with family I'd say we'll face it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the whole plan, take over the firm in ten years, could be tested in two. The office side goes at once, and the supermarkets could buy cheaper from some machine-run supplier. Robots for lorries and warehouses come around 2031, so we'd have three more years, but I'd never trust that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about whether to keep the firm small and local and make our relationships the product. I'd learn the tools, reluctantly, because we'd have no choice. I'd also save, ask my uncle to teach me the driving and warehouse jobs, and keep my degree as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm a person who likes to see how things work, and I'd have no time. Two years is a blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short timescale do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the short time do to you? It takes away the apprenticeship. Normally you learn a trade by watching someone for years. I'd be forced to guess, and I'm not good at guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the government? Help for small firms to adjust, not handouts for people who aren't trying. A grant to train staff and a tax break if you keep people on. That rewards those who stay. Normally you learn a trade by watching someone for years, but with two years I'd be forced to guess.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster waiting** to happen if governments and big firms treat it as a game.
I'd say small firms need **protection** first.
think: The plan to take over the firm would be **tested in two years**.
Supermarkets might buy cheaper from a **machine-run supplier**.
do: Keep the firm small and **local**, and learn the tools reluctantly.
Ask my uncle to teach me **driving and warehouse** jobs.
feel: **Anxious**: he likes to see how things work and would have no time.
S2.quote: Normally you learn a trade by watching someone for years, but with two years I'd be forced to guess.
fieldNote: Diego is **anxious** because the family firm's future is his plan, and he lacks time to learn.
He would rather keep the firm small and relationship-based than chase new tools.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools, however reluctantly, with help from my cousin
Save most of my Saturday pay
Ask my uncle to teach me the driving and warehouse jobs
Ask my parents to keep the firm small and local

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be sensible. I'd tell people it's time to invest in training and in skills you can use anywhere, like running a team and doing the books. I'd say it at the church men's group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but manageable. I'd graduate in 2029, and by 2031 the office jobs would be mostly gone. I could be working in the firm by then, with new systems, and the lorries still running until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and join the firm. I'd do apprenticeships in each job, warehouse, driver and office, so I'd know all of it. I'd learn the tools in year two with a mentor, and I'd start saving so that if something happens, we're not caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. Five years is long enough that I could build something, and short enough that I'd be paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the 2028 version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the 2028 version? I'd have time to learn the tools slowly and carefully, with my dad and my cousin. In the short version I'd do it badly and in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister about her plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister (younger) about her plans? To study something that has a person in it, like teaching or nursing, and to keep a trade as a back-up. She laughs, but it's good advice. Five years is long enough to learn the tools slowly and carefully, and short enough that I'd stay alert.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to be sensible**, so invest in training and portable skills.
I'd say it at the **church men's group**.
think: I'd graduate in **2029**, and by 2031 the office jobs would be mostly gone.
I'd be in the firm with new systems while the **lorries** still run.
do: Finish the degree, join the firm and do **apprenticeships** in each job.
Learn the tools with a **mentor** in year two and save.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady: long enough to build, short enough to pay attention.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn the tools slowly and carefully, and short enough that I'd stay alert.
fieldNote: Diego treats time as a chance to **learn by apprenticeship**, which is how he thinks trades are learned.
His mood is anxious because the firm's office side, where relatives work, is in range.

steps.text: Do short apprenticeships in the warehouse, driving and office jobs
Learn the AI tools in second year with a mentor
Save a fixed amount each month for the firm's reserve
Join the family firm after graduating in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, and anyone who ignores it is making a choice. I'd say work and family come first, and we should meet change with skills and training, not complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. By 2036 I'd be 28, running part of the firm and maybe married. We'd have time to rebuild the office side in a careful way. The lorries and the warehouse wouldn't be touched until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, join the firm, and slowly modernise it, once the tools are proven by others. I'd stay with the family and the church, and keep saving. I'd also train two younger staff into new roles, so no one's job just disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The long view suits me. I like having time to see how things work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid the tools with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you still avoid the tools with ten years to go? I'd keep a distance until they're proven by someone else, and then I'd learn them properly. That's my way. It's slower, but I rarely have to undo a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by 2036? To have kept every member of staff who wanted to stay, and trained the ones whose jobs changed. If I did that, I'd be proud. I'd want to have kept every member of staff who wanted to stay, and trained the ones whose jobs changed.

say: I'd say ten years is **a good length**, and ignoring it is a choice.
I'd say **skills and training**, not complaints, are the answer.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and running **part of the firm**, maybe married.
We'd have time to rebuild the **office side** carefully.
do: Join the firm and **modernise slowly**, once tools are proven by others.
Train **two younger staff** into new roles so no job just disappears.
feel: **Uneasy** only a little: the long view suits him.
S4.quote: I'd want to have kept every member of staff who wanted to stay, and trained the ones whose jobs changed.
fieldNote: Diego's mood is **uneasy**, the family firm still on his mind, but he sees ten years as workable.
His measure of success is loyalty: keeping or retraining every worker who wants to stay.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join the family firm
Train two younger staff for changing office roles
Modernise the firm slowly with tools others have proven
Keep saving a fixed share of my earnings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because a family firm can't change that fast, and neither can I. What would help is something simple: a few years to adjust, support for small firms like ours, and training that's practical, with a person teaching it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like us to remember the people who run small firms and work with their hands, not just the people in offices and banks. They keep the shelves full, and I don't hear them discussed enough. People talk about offices and banks, but it's the family firms with four lorries that keep the shelves full.

headlineQuote: People talk about offices and banks, but it's the family firms with four lorries that keep the shelves full.
portrait: **Diego** is an 18-year-old business student in Birmingham whose parents run a food wholesale firm with four lorries and thirty staff.
He holds **traditional views**: faith, family and work first, with free markets and apprenticeships over handouts.
He has **never used AI tools** and likes to see how a thing works first, which makes him slow to adopt them.
His aim is to take over the **family firm**, so his mood tracks what AI would do to its office and orders.
He blames **big tech** more than workers, and wants practical help for small firms.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, because a family firm cannot change that fast, and neither can he.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **time to adjust**, support for small firms and practical, person-led training.
